title: March deliberations identify when a rise in Canadian petrol prices would require a rate response
summary: Canada entered the energy shock with core inflation approaching 2%, slack in the economy and renewed weakness in employment. In the summary published on 1 April, Governing Council explained why these starting conditions gave it room to hold at 2.25% on 18 March. A higher price at the pump was already a foreseeable consequence of disrupted energy supply. The question for policy was whether pricing and pay elsewhere would continue to rise once the original change in fuel costs passed. Members saw stronger upside risk to inflation and greater downside risk to near-term growth at the same time. Their agreement concerned the immediate decision, while views about the relative importance of the risks differed (Canadian economy and inflation outlook and Policy decision).

Before the shock, the latest inflation release was unusually informative about the distinction. February CPI inflation had fallen to 1.8% from 2.3% in January, as expected in light of the earlier GST holiday dropping out of the annual comparison. Excluding changes in indirect taxes, inflation was 1.9%, and core measures were slowing towards 2%. These figures described conditions before the energy increase. Petrol would soon lift headline inflation, while air travel and food faced possible indirect pressure from fuel, fertiliser and transport. A future higher CPI reading could therefore contain a normalisation in tax comparisons, direct fuel effects and broader price changes with quite different implications for policy (Canadian economy and inflation outlook).

Output data also required a distinction between composition and level. Fourth-quarter GDP had fallen 0.6% after a strong third quarter, with a large inventory adjustment accounting for most of the decline. Final domestic demand was solid and retail indicators suggested consumption continued to expand. New information nevertheless pointed to a weaker first half of 2026 than in January’s Monetary Policy Report. Toronto and Vancouver were prominent in the housing weakness. January goods exports fell as gold, motor vehicles and aircraft shipments declined. Temporary factors explained much of the monthly move, but export growth in the first quarter still looked weaker than the January projection. A stock adjustment and weak export demand have different implications for subsequent production (Canadian economy and inflation outlook).

Employment losses in January and February reversed much of the preceding quarter’s gains. They were broad across industries and concentrated in full-time private-sector jobs, including in wholesale and retail as well as trade-exposed industries. Wage growth remained consistent with earlier expectations. That mix mattered for second-round inflation. Businesses facing soft sales may hesitate to protect margins by raising prices; workers in a less secure labour market may find it harder to negotiate compensation for higher commuting costs. Against that restraint, households had only recently experienced high inflation, and changes in the price of petrol historically had a large influence on perceptions of inflation. Members had reasons both to distinguish the present episode from earlier wage-price spirals and to avoid assuming expectations would remain insensitive (International economy and Considerations for monetary policy).

Canada’s energy trade further complicated the effect on demand. Higher export revenues raise incomes for producers and others connected to energy, while households paying more for petrol and firms facing higher fuel costs reduce real spending elsewhere. Even if the resulting changes in aggregate GDP are small, the industries and regions affected can shift substantially. The Canadian dollar remained just above US$0.73, relatively stable bilaterally while strengthening with the US dollar against most other currencies. Broad financial conditions had tightened from accommodative levels, with higher yields and wider credit spreads, but markets remained orderly. Currency and financing conditions could either modify or amplify the trade and income channels. The summary supplies no quantitative net energy multiplier or measured market reaction to the decision (International economy and Canadian economy and inflation outlook).

The international outlook also contained a separate trade risk. The US court ruling concerning emergency-powers tariffs and the administration’s plans for alternatives did not directly change existing sectoral tariffs affecting Canada. The forthcoming North American trade agreement review was still important to investment and export decisions. US demand and AI investment remained supportive, whereas the euro area and much of Asia were especially exposed to imported energy. Council saw a material difference between a short-lived shipping disruption and one that spread through fertiliser, production and transport networks. Lower oil use per unit of global output reduced one historical source of pass-through, but the result still depended on the duration of the disruption and the behaviour of households and firms (International economy).

The policy trade-off was clear. Tightening to offset direct fuel effects would reduce demand in an economy already in excess supply, while easing to insure against weaker growth could accommodate lasting price increases. Council intended to look through the immediate rise and respond if it spread more broadly or persisted. Members discussed using firm-level price data, direct business outreach, timely indicators and scenarios to tell these paths apart. This stage-three summary was released after the decision and reports views collectively. It contains no numerical vote split or commitment to a particular next move. In a historical event study the announcement and the later document explaining this judgement constitute different information dates (Considerations for monetary policy and Policy decision).

questions.question: Did petrol-price exposure change what non-energy businesses actually charged?
questions.detail: Compare firms facing similar fuel and freight costs but different local sales conditions. Track their intended and realised selling prices, margins and volumes. Control for the earlier GST effects and separately identify products with direct energy exposure. A short-lived increase in households’ headline inflation expectations does not by itself establish that firms found it easier to pass costs through.

questions.question: How quickly did energy export income offset purchasing-power losses for Canadian households?
questions.detail: Track export receipts, investment, payrolls and household consumption in energy-producing regions alongside spending by fuel-intensive households elsewhere. Allow for the time between export receipts and domestic investment or distributions. Use both bilateral and trade-weighted exchange rates, because a stable Canadian dollar against the US dollar can coexist with appreciation against other suppliers.

questions.question: Did markets revise the expected rate path after learning Council’s criteria for a response?
questions.detail: Measure short-dated Canadian rate expectations separately around the 18 March decision and the 1 April summary. Identify simultaneous changes in oil, US rates and tariff news. Compare any repricing with newly published information about excess supply, expectations and the risk of pass-through. Returns between the two dates combine many shocks and cannot identify the effect of the deliberations.
